item.text: {"text":"Evidence supports text sharing for sparse items, but does not establish the exact proposed architecture. [TASTE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.14029) reports improved long-tail recommendation and reduced popularity bias; [Recformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13731) reports strong cold-start and low-resource results. Both use pretrained language representations, so their gains cannot be assumed for randomly initialized, mean-pooled tokens trained only on recommendation interactions. [TedRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18166) also cautions that directly adding text and ID embeddings can be ineffective because their representation characteristics differ. These findings motivate testing lexical sharing, rather than treating its benefit as established.\n\nNo directly matching controlled evidence for brand-token shortcut learning surfaced in this search. Brand overlap may represent legitimate preference or superficial similarity; aggregate HR@10 cannot distinguish them. Suggested experiments, rather than published conclusions: compare matched HSTU models using ID-only embeddings versus ID plus a learned, gated residual from mean-pooled title/description tokens; train both from scratch with the same protocol. Add separately trained controls with item-to-text assignments shuffled and with identifiable brand/name tokens removed from available text. Measure validation HR@10 by training-item frequency and history–target lexical overlap, alongside the required macro score. Improvements concentrated in rare items and surviving brand removal would strengthen the lexical-sharing explanation; gains reproduced by shuffled text would suggest capacity or regularization effects. Each variant should remain one jointly trained network per category, with no score fusion or checkpoint averaging."}
